mainTopic: End of the משנה (stones of a fallen wall; paying a פועל with hay and straw) and the opening of the גמרא: the מחלוקת between רב and שמואל on how big a break in the roof of the בית הבד must be, and why that מחלוקת had to be stated in two places.
overview: The amud opens at the end of a משנה. If a wall falls into a neighbor's garden, its owner cannot force the stones on the neighbor, and an employer cannot force a פועל to take the hay or straw he worked on as pay. But once the other side accepts, the deal cannot be undone. The גמרא then explains the earlier case of a בית הבד whose roof broke: רב says most of it must break, שמואל says four טפחים is enough, and their מחלוקת had to be taught both here and for a house. רבי יוחנן says the court's standard time to remove a danger is thirty days. The גמרא shows that the garden owner gets the stones only if he cleared them, because a field acquires only when the giver truly means to give. It explains why both cases of the משנה were needed. It then settles a contradiction between the משנה and a ברייתא about paying in straw: after רבא knocks down two answers, רב נחמן distinguishes lifting from merely watching. Finally רבה and רבא give different readings of a משנה about guards of שמיטה grain: is the argument about whether watching acquires ownerless property, about trusting an unpaid guard, or about scaring off violent people?

steps.title: The fallen stones: before and after the garden owner accepts them
steps.stepSummary: The wall owner cannot force the stones on the garden owner. But once the garden owner accepts them, the wall owner cannot pay his costs and take the stones back.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the wall owner says 'The stones are yours,' we do not listen to him. If the garden owner already accepted them, and then the wall owner says 'Here is what you spent, and I'll take my stones,' we do not listen to him either.
steps.whatsHappening: We are joining the משנה in the middle. It is finishing the case of a wall that fell into a neighbor's garden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before acceptance, the wall owner cannot push his stones (and the job of clearing them) onto his neighbor just by giving them up. After the garden owner accepts them, they belong to him. Offering to repay his expenses does not undo that.

keyTerms.meaning: They have reached you, meaning they are yours now
We (the court) do not listen to him
Once he accepted it upon himself

phrases.english: They have reached you (they're yours) —
we do not listen to him.
Once he (the garden owner) accepted it upon himself,
if he (the wall owner) said to him: Here are your expenses,
and I will take what is mine —
we do not listen to him.

steps.mimraCoreRuling: An owner cannot force his fallen stones on a neighbor. Once the neighbor accepts them, they are his and cannot be taken back.

steps.title: Paying a worker with the hay he worked on
steps.stepSummary: An employer cannot force a פועל to take hay or straw as his wages. Once the worker accepts it, the employer cannot change his mind and take it back.
steps.simpleTranslation: Someone hires a worker to work with hay and straw. The worker asks for his pay, and the employer says, 'Take some of what you worked on as your pay.' We do not listen to the employer. If the worker already accepted it, and then the employer says, 'Here is your pay in money, and I'll take back my hay,' we do not listen to him either.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives a second case that works the same way as the stones: before agreement, the employer cannot force it; after agreement, he cannot undo it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A worker is owed his wages in the form they agreed on, so the employer cannot pay him in hay or straw against his will. But once the worker accepts the hay, he owns it, and the employer cannot swap it back for money.
steps.whatToRemember: In both cases of the משנה, one side cannot force a payment or a transfer on the other. Once the other side accepts it, though, it is final.

phrases.english: One who hires a worker
to work for him with hay and with straw,
and he (the worker) said to him: Give me my wages.

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר לוֹ: טוֹל מַה שֶּׁעָשִׂית בִּשְׂכָרְךָ –
phrases.english: And he (the employer) said to him: Take what you worked on as your wages —
we do not listen to him.
Once he (the worker) accepted it upon himself,
and he (the employer) said to him: Here are your wages,
and I will take what is mine —
we do not listen to him.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַשּׂוֹכֵר אֶת הַפּוֹעֵל לַעֲשׂוֹת עִמּוֹ בַּתֶּבֶן וּבַקַּשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel case following the same pattern as the stones.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A worker cannot be forced to take produce as wages. Once he accepts it, the employer cannot take it back.

steps.title: How big a break counts: רב versus שמואל
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens on the משנה's case of the olive press whose roof broke. רב says most of the roof must have fallen in; שמואל says a hole of four טפחים is enough.
steps.simpleTranslation: About the words 'it broke through': רב says this means most of it broke, and שמואל says it means a hole of four handbreadths.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins. It asks what size break the משנה is talking about in the case of the בית הבד with a garden on top.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In that משנה, once the roof breaks, the garden owner may go down and plant below until the press owner builds a new roof. רב and שמואל argue about how much must break before this rule applies.

phrases.english: GEMARA
'It broke through' —
phrases.notes: This goes back to the משנה's case of an olive press with a garden on top whose roof broke.

phrases.english: Rav says: through most of it,
and Shmuel says: through four (handbreadths).

steps.triggerLanguage: נִפְחֲתָה, רַב אָמַר בְּרוּבָּהּ, וּשְׁמוּאֵל אָמַר בְּאַרְבַּע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the end of the משנה and goes back to an earlier case in it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב: the rule applies only when most of the roof broke. שמואל: a break of four טפחים is enough.

steps.title: The reasons behind each view
steps.stepSummary: רב holds that with only a four-טפחים hole, a person can still plant partly below and partly above. שמואל holds that people do not plant that way.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב says it must be most of it, because with only four handbreadths a person can sow half below and half above. שמואל says four is enough, because a person does not sow half below and half above.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why each of them sets the size where he does.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is whether a small hole really stops the garden owner from planting normally. רב says he can manage, planting most of his garden up top and a bit in the hole, so only a large collapse counts. שמואל says splitting a garden between two levels is not normal, so even four טפחים is enough to count.

phrases.english: Rav says: through most of it,
but with four (handbreadths) —
a person does sow part of it below
and part of it above.
And Shmuel says: with four —
a person does not sow part of it below
and part of it above.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָמַר: בְּרוּבָּהּ, אֲבָל בְּאַרְבַּע – אָדָם זוֹרֵעַ חֶצְיוֹ לְמַטָּה וְחֶצְיוֹ לְמַעְלָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reasoning behind the two positions just stated.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The argument depends on whether people normally plant on two levels at once.

steps.title: Why the house case alone would not be enough
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins explaining why the רב–שמואל מחלוקת had to be stated both for the house and for the olive press. From the house case alone, we might think שמואל would agree with רב about planting.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was necessary to teach both. If we had only been taught about living in a house, we might say שמואל holds his view there because people don't live a little here and a little there. But when it comes to planting, people do plant a little here and a little there, so we might think שמואל agrees with רב.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא notices that רב and שמואל argue about the same thing in an earlier case (a house with an upper floor that broke). It starts explaining why we need to hear the argument twice. This is the first half; the second half comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Living split between two floors is clearly unusual, so שמואל's strict view fits a house well. Planting in scattered patches is more common, so without this second case we might have thought שמואל agrees with רב about the garden.

keyTerms.meaning: It is necessary (to state both cases)

phrases.english: And it is necessary (to state both):
for if it had taught us only about living in a house,
phrases.notes: This is the earlier case in the פרק of a house with an upper floor that broke, where רב and שמואל argue the same way.

phrases.english: in this case Shmuel says his view
because people do not usually
live a little here and a little there,
but regarding sowing —
people do usually
sow a little here and a little there,
I might say he (Shmuel) agrees with Rav.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Compares this מחלוקת to the same מחלוקת in the house case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The house case alone would not show that שמואל holds his view about planting too.

steps.title: Why the olive press case alone would not be enough
steps.stepSummary: From the olive press case alone, we might think רב agrees with שמואל about a house. So both cases are needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if it had been said only about this case (the press), we might say רב holds his view here, but about the house he agrees with שמואל. So both are necessary.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the reasoning by looking at it from רב's side, and concludes that both statements are needed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב's lenient view fits planting, since people do plant in patches. Living split between floors is less normal, so without the house case we might think רב agrees with שמואל there. Each case teaches that one of the two אמוראים holds his view even where it is less obvious.
steps.whatToRemember: רב (most of it) and שמואל (four טפחים) argue in both cases, the house and the olive press. Each case is needed so we know that each of them holds his view in both settings.

phrases.english: And if it had been stated only in this one,
phrases.notes: 'This one' is the olive press and garden; 'that one' in the next lines is the house.

phrases.english: in this one Rav says his view,
but in that one —
I might say he (Rav) agrees with Shmuel,
so it is necessary (to state both).

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי אִיתְּמַר בְּהָךְ, בְּהָךְ קָאָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the other half of the צריכותא started in step 5.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The מחלוקת had to be stated in both cases, because each case alone would leave room to think one Amora agrees with the other in the other case.

steps.title: How much time does the court give?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's words 'they gave him time' and asks how long that standard time is.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'They gave him time.' How long is the usual time a court gives?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a phrase from the משנה about a shaky wall or leaning tree and asks a simple factual question: how many days does the בית דין give? This sets up רבי יוחנן's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says that if the owner was given time and the wall or tree fell during that time, he is exempt. After that time, he is liable. So we need to know exactly how long 'the time' is, because it decides when he becomes liable.

keyTerms.meaning: Time; here, a set period the court gives to fix the danger

phrases.english: "They gave him time."
phrases.notes: These are words from the משנה: the court gave the owner time to cut down his leaning tree or take down his shaky wall.

phrases.english: And how much is the time of a court?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to a new line of the משנה, after the house and olive press discussion is finished.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The standard length of time a בית דין gives an owner to remove a danger.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: thirty days
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן answers that the court's standard time is thirty days.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן says: thirty days.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן answers the question from the last step. The standard time a court gives is thirty days.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the משנה's rule is clear. If the wall or tree falls within thirty days, the owner is exempt. If it falls after the thirty days are over, he is liable.

keyTerms.meaning: A leading אמורא of ארץ ישראל

steps.whatToRemember: The standard 'time from בית דין' is thirty days.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yoḥanan said:
Thirty days.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 7.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The court's standard time is thirty days.

steps.title: Inference: the stones are his only because he cleared them
steps.stepSummary: From the משנה's last clause, 'here are your expenses,' the גמרא infers that the case is one where the garden owner cleared the stones. If he had not cleared them, they would not be his.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'One whose wall fell into his friend's garden...' Since the end of the משנה says the wall owner offers, 'Here are your expenses,' we see that we are dealing with a case where the garden owner cleared the stones away. So the reason the stones stay with the garden owner is that he cleared them. If he did not clear them, they would not be his.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא turns to a new case in the משנה. A wall fell into a neighbor's garden, and the wall owner said, 'Keep the stones.' The גמרא reads the end of the משנה closely to work out exactly what the case is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says that if the wall owner later offers, 'Here are your expenses, give me back my stones,' we do not listen to him. 'Expenses' only make sense if the garden owner spent effort clearing the stones. So the wall owner cannot take back his words only because the garden owner cleared them. Without the clearing, the stones would still belong to the wall owner.

keyTerms.meaning: The last clause of a משנה
"Here are your expenses": an offer to pay back the cost of clearing

steps.confusionAlert: 'הא לא פנינהו – לא' does not mean the garden owner is forced to clear them. It means that if he did not clear them, the stones are not his. They still belong to the wall owner.

phrases.english: "One whose wall," etc.
Now, since the last clause teaches:
"Here are your expenses,"
it follows that we are dealing with a case where he cleared them.
The reason is that he cleared them;
but if he did not clear them, no.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new section of the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The garden owner keeps the stones only because he cleared them. If he did not clear them, they stay with the wall owner.

steps.title: Shouldn't his field acquire the stones for him?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the inference: the garden owner's field should acquire the stones automatically, since a person's courtyard acquires for him even without his knowledge.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why is that? His field should acquire the stones for him! After all, רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא said: a person's courtyard acquires things for him even without his knowledge.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the conclusion of step 9. Even if the garden owner did not clear the stones, they are lying in his field, and his field should acquire them for him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a known rule, קנין חצר: a person's property acquires items for him, even if he does not know about them. The stones are sitting in the garden, and the wall owner said 'keep them.' So why should clearing matter at all?

keyTerms.meaning: An אמורא who teaches the rule of קנין חצר

phrases.english: Why? Let his field acquire them for him,
as Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Ḥanina, said:
A person's courtyard acquires for him
even without his knowledge!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the inference of step 9.
steps.kashyaTarget: The inference that without clearing, the stones are not the garden owner's.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: By the rule of קנין חצר, the field itself should acquire the stones, so clearing should not be needed.

steps.title: A field acquires only when the giver means to give
steps.stepSummary: קנין חצר works only when the giver intends to transfer ownership. Here the wall owner was only dodging the work, not really giving the stones.
steps.simpleTranslation: That rule applies only where the giver means to give the item to him. But here, the wall owner is just trying to get out of the work.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. It limits the rule of קנין חצר to cases where the giver really wants to give.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A field can acquire for its owner only when someone is actually giving him the item. When the wall owner said 'keep the stones,' he did not mean it as a gift. He was dodging the neighbor so that the neighbor would clear them, and then he could take them back easily. Since no real giving happened, the field acquires nothing. Only the actual clearing makes the stones the garden owner's.
steps.whatToRemember: קנין חצר acquires for a person only when the giver truly means to give. Words said only to dodge someone are not a gift.
steps.whyThisMatters: This answer sets a limit on קנין חצר: a person's property can acquire for him only when someone is actually giving the item, not when the 'giver' is just brushing him off.

phrases.english: These words apply only where
he intends to transfer ownership to him.

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל הָכָא – אִישְׁתְּמוֹטֵי הוּא דְּקָא מִישְׁתְּמִיט לֵיהּ.
phrases.english: But here, he is just evading him.
phrases.notes: The wall owner wants his neighbor to do the clearing, so he can collect the stones easily later. He never meant to give them away.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָנֵי מִילֵּי הֵיכָא דְּקָא מִיכַּוֵּין לְאַקְנוֹיֵי לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 10 and keeps the inference of step 9 in place.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the scope of a rule (קנין חצר needs the giver's intent)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A field always acquires items in it for its owner, so the stones should be his even without clearing.
steps.terutzMaskana: A field acquires only when the giver means to give. Here the wall owner was dodging, so only the clearing makes the stones the garden owner's.

steps.title: Quoting the straw case and announcing that both cases are needed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה about hiring a worker to work with straw and states that both this case and the stones case are necessary.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'One who hires a worker to work with him with straw, etc.' And both cases are necessary.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next case of the משנה and announces that it will explain why both cases had to be taught. This is a setup line for the explanation that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two cases in the משנה look alike. In both, one person offers the other the material itself ('they are yours'), and the court does not listen to him. The word צריכא tells us the גמרא will now show that we could not have learned one case from the other.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Etc.' The quote goes on in the משנה
It is necessary. The גמרא is about to explain why both cases had to be taught

phrases.english: One who hires [a worker] to do work with him with straw, etc.
And it is necessary [to teach both cases].

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from the stones discussion (steps 9-11) to the next case in the משנה, and announces a צריכותא linking the two cases.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Both the stones case and the straw case are needed. Neither one could have been learned from the other.

steps.title: Why the stones case alone would not teach the straw case
steps.stepSummary: If the משנה had taught only the stones case, we might think the court ignores 'they are yours' only because no wages were owed. In the straw case wages are owed, so we might have thought the court accepts payment in straw.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the משנה had taught only the first case, that when the wall owner says 'they are yours' we do not listen to him, I would say that is because the garden owner is owed no wages. But here, where the worker is owed wages, I would say we do listen to the employer, as people say: 'From your debtor, take even bran as payment.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the first half of the צריכותא. It explains why we could not learn the straw case from the stones case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the stones case, the garden owner was never owed anything. So it makes sense that he cannot be forced to take stones. In the straw case, the worker is owed money, and the saying teaches that a creditor should take whatever he can get. So without the משנה we might have said the worker must accept the straw.

keyTerms.meaning: 'They have reached you,' meaning 'they are yours'
We (the court) do not listen to him
A saying: from your debtor, collect even bran

phrases.english: For if it had taught us only that first case,
phrases.notes: The 'first case' is the fallen wall whose stones landed in the neighbor's garden.

phrases.english: that when he says to him, "They are yours,"
we do not listen to him,
[I would say that is] because he has no wages owed to him by the other.

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל הָכָא, דְּאִית לֵיהּ אַגְרָא גַּבֵּיהּ
phrases.english: But here, where he does have wages owed to him,
I would say we do listen to him,
as people say:
"From your debtor, collect even bran."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the first half of the צריכותא announced in step 12.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The stones case alone would not teach the straw case, because in the straw case a debt of wages exists and one might think a creditor must take whatever is offered.

steps.title: Why the straw case alone would not teach the stones case
steps.stepSummary: If the משנה had taught only the straw case, we might think the employer cannot take back his offer once the worker accepted only because wages are owed. In the stones case no wages are owed, so we might have thought the wall owner can take it back. Therefore both cases are needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if the משנה had taught only the straw case, I would say that here, once the worker accepted the straw, we do not listen to the employer who wants to take it back, because wages are owed. But in the stones case, where no wages are owed, I would say we do listen to him. So both are necessary.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the second half of the צריכותא, now looking at the second part of each case: after the offer was accepted. It ends by declaring that both cases are necessary.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This half is about the moment after the other person accepted the offer (משקיבל עליו). In the straw case, the employer cannot take the straw back, since it is standing in for wages he really owes. In the stones case, nothing was owed, so we might think the wall owner could change his mind. The משנה teaches that even there, once the garden owner accepted, the wall owner cannot take it back.

keyTerms.meaning: Once he accepted it upon himself
I would say (what we might have mistakenly thought)

steps.whatToRemember: Each case has its own reason. In the straw case wages are owed; in the stones case they are not. That difference could have changed the law either way, so the משנה had to teach both cases.
steps.confusionAlert: Each half of the צריכותא is about a different part of the case. The first half is about the first offer ('they are yours' gets ignored). The second half is about after the offer was accepted (the giver cannot take it back).

phrases.english: And if it had taught us only here [the straw case],

phrases.aramaic: – הָכָא שֶׁמִּשֶּׁקִּבֵּל עָלָיו אֵין שׁוֹמְעִין לוֹ,
phrases.english: [I would say] here, once he accepted it, we do not listen to him [when he wants to take it back],
because he has wages owed to him.

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל הָכָא, דְּלֵית לֵיהּ אַגְרָא גַּבֵּיהּ
phrases.english: But here [the stones case], where he has no wages owed to him,
I would say we do listen to him. So both are necessary.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the צריכותא begun in step 13 by showing the opposite direction.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The straw case alone would not teach the stones case, because without owed wages one might think the giver can take back his offer even after it was accepted.

steps.title: A ברייתא says the court does listen to the employer
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's ruling that we do not listen to the employer who pays in straw, and challenges it with a ברייתא that says we do listen to him.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'We do not listen to him.' But a ברייתא teaches: 'We do listen to him!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets the משנה's ruling against a ברייתא that says the opposite.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says an employer cannot force his worker to take straw as pay. The ברייתא seems to say he can. Both are authoritative sources, so the גמרא needs to explain how both can be true.

keyTerms.meaning: But isn't it taught (in a ברייתא)? This introduces a contradicting source
We (the court) do listen to him

phrases.english: "We do not listen to him."
But isn't it taught [in a ברייתא]: "We do listen to him"!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the צריכותא and opens a new question: a contradiction between the משנה and a ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that the court does not listen to an employer who offers straw as wages.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא rules the exact opposite, that the court does listen to him.

steps.title: רב נחמן: the employer's own straw versus someone else's
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן says there is no contradiction. The משנה is about work done with the employer's own straw, and the ברייתא is about work done with someone else's straw.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said: It is not difficult. Here (the משנה) is about his own straw; there (the ברייתא) is about another person's straw.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן resolves the contradiction by saying the two sources are talking about two different cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the straw belongs to the employer, the court does not listen to him, as the משנה says. When the work was done with straw belonging to someone else, the court does listen to him, as the ברייתא says. So the two sources do not argue. Each one rules on its own case.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult. There is no real contradiction
An אמורא who gives the answer here

steps.whatToRemember: The משנה (we do not listen) is about the employer's own straw. The ברייתא (we do listen) is about straw belonging to someone else.

phrases.english: Rav Nachman said: It is not difficult.
Here, with his own [straw];
phrases.notes: 'Here' means the משנה, where the court does not listen to the employer.

phrases.english: there, with another person's [straw].

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן: לָא קַשְׁיָא. כָּאן בְּשֶׁלּוֹ, כָּאן בְּשֶׁל חֲבֵירוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 15.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): each source is about a different situation.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה and the ברייתא disagree about whether an employer can pay his worker with straw.
steps.terutzMaskana: No disagreement: the משנה is about the employer's own straw, and the ברייתא is about straw belonging to someone else.

steps.title: רבא: the employer owes the wage even for work on someone else's property
steps.stepSummary: רבא argues that רב נחמן's split between 'his own straw' and 'his friend's straw' does not work, because in both cases the wage is the employer's responsibility.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to רב נחמן: When the straw is the employer's own, why does the court not listen to him? Because the worker says, 'Paying my wage is your job.' But when it is his friend's straw, paying the wage is also the employer's job!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא attacks רב נחמן's answer from step 16. He says the reason behind the משנה applies just as well to someone else's straw.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה's reason is that the worker can say 'my wage is your responsibility,' so he does not have to take straw. רבא points out that this is equally true when the straw belongs to someone else, since the employer is still the one who hired him. So the difference רב נחמן drew does not change anything. רבא's proof comes in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: The wage is on you (your responsibility to pay)

phrases.english: Rava said to Rav Nachman:
With his own [straw], what is the reason [the court ignores him]?
Because [the worker] says to him: The wage is on you.
With his friend's [straw], too, his wage is on [the employer].

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב נחמן's resolution from step 16.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב נחמן's distinction between the employer's own straw and his friend's straw.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The reason the court ignores the employer (the wage is his duty) applies equally when the straw is someone else's, so the distinction does not explain why the ברייתא lets him pay in straw.

steps.title: Proof: the employer pays a worker who worked in someone else's field
steps.stepSummary: רבא cites a ברייתא: if an employer sent his worker to the wrong field, he still pays the full wage himself and then collects the benefit from that field's owner.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is taught: Someone hired a worker to work in his own field and showed him his friend's field by mistake. He gives the worker his full wage, and then goes back and collects from the field's owner the value of the benefit he gave him.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא backs up his challenge with a ברייתא. It shows that the wage stays the employer's responsibility even when the work was done on someone else's property.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The worker does not chase the field owner for his pay. The employer pays the full wage and then settles up with the field owner himself. That proves 'the wage is on you' applies even with someone else's property, so רב נחמן's answer falls.

keyTerms.meaning: As it is taught (in a ברייתא)

phrases.english: As it is taught:
One who hires a worker to work in his own [field],
and he showed him [a field] of his friend,
gives him his wage in full,
and goes back and takes from the owner [of the field]
what [the work] benefited him!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the source for רבא's challenge in step 17.
steps.raayaObject: That the employer owes the wage even when the work was done with someone else's property.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about an employer who showed his worker the wrong field.

steps.title: רב נחמן's new answer: own straw versus ownerless straw
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן drops his earlier answer. Now the משנה is about the employer's own straw, and the ברייתא is about ownerless (הפקר) straw.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רב נחמן said: It is not difficult. Here it is his own straw; there it is ownerless straw.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן gives a new way to settle the contradiction between the משנה and the ברייתא, replacing the one רבא knocked down.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the employer pays with his own straw, the worker can say 'I want money, not your straw.' If the worker was hired to gather ownerless straw, the employer can tell him to keep some of it as pay, since it never really belonged to the employer. The word אלא tells us the earlier answer is dropped.

keyTerms.meaning: Here... there (each source is about a different case)

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two answers. The first contrast was 'own straw vs. a friend's straw.' The new one is 'own straw vs. ownerless straw.'

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן, לָא קַשְׁיָא:
phrases.english: Rather, Rav Nachman said: It is not difficult:
Here, with his own [straw],
phrases.notes: 'Here' means the משנה, where the court ignores the employer.

phrases.english: there, with ownerless [straw].

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן, לָא קַשְׁיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the answer rejected in steps 17-18.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): each source is about a different kind of straw.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא was about someone else's straw.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא is about ownerless straw, which the employer can give the worker as pay.

steps.title: רבא: a hired worker's finds go to the employer
steps.stepSummary: רבא cites a ברייתא: a worker hired for general work picks up found items for his employer. So ownerless straw the worker gathers would belong to the employer.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא objected to רב נחמן: A worker's find belongs to himself. When is that? When the employer told him, 'Weed with me today,' or 'Hoe with me today.' But if he told him, 'Do work with me today,' his find belongs to the employer!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא attacks רב נחמן's new answer with another ברייתא, this one about who owns what a hired worker finds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the employer hired the worker for open-ended 'work,' picking things up counts as part of the job, so the worker's finds belong to the employer. A worker hired to gather ownerless straw is certainly doing that as his job, so the straw becomes the employer's own. That puts it back in the משנה's case, where the employer cannot pay in straw.

keyTerms.meaning: He raised an objection to him (from a ברייתא)

phrases.english: Rava raised an objection to Rav Nachman:
A worker's find belongs to himself. When?
When the employer told him:
Weed with me today,
or hoe with me today.
But if he told him:
Do work with me today,
his find belongs to the employer!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב נחמן's second answer from step 19.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב נחמן's claim that the ברייתא is about ownerless straw.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A worker hired to gather ownerless straw acquires it for his employer, as a worker's finds do. So the straw is the employer's own, and he should not be able to force it on the worker as pay.

steps.title: Final answer: lifting the straw versus just watching it
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן says both sources are about ownerless straw. In the משנה the worker lifted it (הגבהה), so it became the employer's. In the ברייתא he only watched over it (הבטה), so it stayed ownerless.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רב נחמן said: It is not difficult. Here, it is with lifting; there, it is with looking.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן gives his third and final answer, which handles רבא's objection about the worker's finds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Lifting an ownerless item is how a person acquires it. A worker hired to lift the straw does that for his employer, so the straw becomes the employer's, and the משנה's rule applies. A worker hired only to look after the straw never acquires it, so it stays ownerless, and the employer can tell him to take some as pay, as the ברייתא says.

keyTerms.meaning: Looking or watching (does not take ownership)

steps.whatToRemember: Three answers to the משנה-versus-ברייתא contradiction: (1) own straw vs. a friend's straw, which fails because the wage is still the employer's duty; (2) own straw vs. ownerless straw, which fails because a worker's finds go to the employer; (3) lifting vs. watching, the final answer. Only lifting makes the ownerless straw the employer's.
steps.whyThisMatters: רב נחמן's answer assumes that just looking at an ownerless item does not acquire it, while lifting does, and a hired worker can lift it on his employer's behalf. The next steps show this assumption is not simple: רבה calls it a dispute of תנאים.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן, לָא קַשְׁיָא:
phrases.english: Rather, Rav Nachman said: It is not difficult:
Here, with lifting,
phrases.notes: 'Here' is the משנה: the worker picked up the straw, so it became the employer's.

phrases.english: there, with looking.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן, לָא קַשְׁיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבא's objection in step 20 by refining the ownerless-straw case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא) by type of work: lifting vs. watching.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any ownerless straw the worker handled would belong to the employer.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only straw the worker lifted becomes the employer's. Straw he only watched stays ownerless and can be given as pay.

steps.title: רבה: Watching Ownerless Property Is a Dispute of תנאים
steps.stepSummary: רבה says that whether הבטה acquires הפקר is already argued about by תנאים.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה says: Whether watching over ownerless property acquires it is a dispute between תנאים.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה makes a new claim: the question from the last step, whether simply watching ownerless items makes them yours, is an old argument between תנאים. He is about to bring the source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 21 רב נחמן assumed that הבטה does not acquire הפקר. רבה now says this is not a simple fact. It depends on which תנא you follow, so רב נחמן's answer only works according to one side.

keyTerms.meaning: Looking at / watching over an item (as opposed to lifting it)
It is a dispute between תנאים

phrases.english: Rabba says:
Watching over ownerless property, whether it acquires, is a dispute of Tannaim.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה: הַבָּטָה בְּהֶפְקֵר – תַּנָּאֵי הִיא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Picks up רב נחמן's idea that הבטה does not acquire and claims it is a תנאים dispute.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Whether הבטה בהפקר acquires is disputed by תנאים.

steps.title: The משנה About Guards of Sabbatical Aftergrowth
steps.stepSummary: רבה quotes a משנה: guards of שביעית aftergrowth are paid from Temple funds. רבי יוסי says one may guard for free, and the חכמים object.
steps.simpleTranslation: As we learned: The guards of the Sabbatical aftergrowth take their wages from the Temple chamber's collection. רבי יוסי says: Whoever wishes may volunteer and guard for free. They said to him: You say so? Then they do not come from communal property!
steps.whatsHappening: רבה brings the source for his claim: a משנה about the people who guard the wild grain of שמיטה so it can be used for the Temple's communal offerings.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ת״ק says the guards must be paid from public Temple money. רבי יוסי says a volunteer is fine. The חכמים object that with a volunteer, the offerings would not come from the community. That is a problem because the עומר and שתי הלחם must belong to the whole community.

keyTerms.meaning: Grain that grew on its own during the שמיטה year
The communal fund collected in the Temple chamber (from the half-שקל)

phrases.english: As we learned in a Mishnah:
The guards of the aftergrowth of the Sabbatical Year
phrases.notes: This is the grain kept safe so it could be used for the עומר and the two loaves.

phrases.english: take their wages from the Temple chamber's collection.
Rabbi Yosei says:
Whoever wishes may volunteer and guard for free.
They said to him: You say so?
They do not come from the community's property!
phrases.notes: "They" means the עומר and the two loaves, which must belong to the whole community.

steps.triggerLanguage: דִּתְנַן: שׁוֹמְרֵי סְפִיחֵי שְׁבִיעִית נוֹטְלִין שְׂכָרָן מִתְּרוּמַת הַלִּשְׁכָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the משנה that רבה says shows the תנאים dispute.
steps.raayaObject: רבה's claim that הבטה בהפקר is a תנאים dispute.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה in שקלים about guards of ספיחי שביעית.

steps.title: Reading the Dispute as About Whether Watching Acquires
steps.stepSummary: The ת״ק holds הבטה acquires, so the guard must be paid to acquire for the community. רבי יוסי holds הבטה does not acquire, so the community only acquires when it gathers the grain.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is it not about this that they disagree? The תנא קמא holds that watching ownerless property acquires it. So if they pay him, yes, it is the community's, and if not, no. רבי יוסי holds that watching does not acquire, so when the community goes and brings the grain, only then do they acquire it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains how the משנה shows a dispute about הבטה. Each opinion is tied to one side of the question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If watching acquires (ת״ק), an unpaid guard acquires the grain for himself, and then the offering is not communal. So he must be a paid worker of the community. If watching does not acquire (רבי יוסי), the guard never owns it. The community acquires it when they harvest, so a volunteer causes no problem.

keyTerms.meaning: Is it not about this that they argue? (proposing the root of a dispute)
The first, unnamed opinion in a משנה

phrases.english: Is it not about this that they argue:
that the first Tanna holds
watching ownerless property acquires it,
and if they give him a wage, yes,
phrases.notes: Meaning: if he is paid, he acquires it for the community.

phrases.english: and if not, no.
And Rabbi Yosei holds
watching ownerless property does not acquire it,
and when the community goes and brings it,
only now do they acquire it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Interprets the משנה from step 23 to support רבה's claim.
steps.raayaObject: That הבטה בהפקר is disputed by תנאים.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ת״ק and רבי יוסי in the ספיחי שביעית משנה.

steps.title: What Did the Rabbis Mean by 'You Say So'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how to understand the חכמים's words "אתה אומר כן" under this reading.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what does "You say so?" mean?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a clarifying question. If רבי יוסי holds that watching does not acquire, why did the חכמים object to him at all? The answer comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under רבי יוסי's own view, a volunteer causes no problem, since he never acquires the grain. So the חכמים's objection seems to miss his point, and the גמרא needs to explain it.

keyTerms.meaning: "You say?", the חכמים's challenge to רבי יוסי

phrases.english: And what is the meaning of "You say so?"

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks how the חכמים's reply fits the reading in step 24.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How the חכמים's objection makes sense if רבי יוסי holds הבטה does not acquire.

steps.title: Combining His Ruling With Our View
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים meant: if we combine your ruling (a volunteer is fine) with our view (הבטה acquires), the offerings would not be communal.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what they said to him: Taking your words together with our words, the עומר and the two loaves would not come from communal property.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the חכמים were not attacking רבי יוסי's own logic. They were explaining why they cannot accept his ruling, given their own view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The חכמים hold that הבטה acquires. If they allowed volunteers as רבי יוסי does, the volunteer would own the grain, and the offerings would not be communal. So "you say so?" means "your ruling cannot work with our principle."

keyTerms.meaning: From your words to ours: applying your ruling within our view
The barley offering of פסח and the two wheat loaves of שבועות, both communal offerings

phrases.english: This is what they were saying to him:
From your words to our words,
phrases.notes: He means: if we used your ruling while keeping our view that watching acquires.

phrases.english: the Omer and the two loaves would not
come from the community's property.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 25.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The חכמים were applying רבי יוסי's ruling to their own principle that הבטה acquires, which would make the offerings not communal.
steps.whatToRemember: According to רבה: ת״ק says הבטה acquires, so the guard must be paid. רבי יוסי says הבטה does not acquire, so a volunteer is fine.

steps.title: רבא: Everyone Agrees Watching Acquires; The Worry Is Wholehearted Transfer
steps.stepSummary: רבא rejects רבה's reading. All agree הבטה acquires. The dispute is whether we fear an unpaid guard will not hand the grain over wholeheartedly. The חכמים say pay him because of this worry.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: No. Everyone agrees that watching ownerless property acquires it. Here they argue about whether we worry that perhaps he will not hand them over wholeheartedly. The Rabbis hold that we give him a wage, because if not, we worry that perhaps he will not hand them over wholeheartedly.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא pushes back on רבה and offers a different reason for the argument in the משנה. He begins by explaining the חכמים's side.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא removes the question of הבטה from the dispute: both sides agree watching acquires. The real issue is a practical worry. An unpaid guard may feel the grain is really his and give it to the community only halfheartedly. The חכמים fear this, so they require a wage.

keyTerms.meaning: Hand them over fully and wholeheartedly

steps.confusionAlert: רבא is not saying that הבטה fails to acquire. He says the opposite: everyone agrees it acquires. The argument is only about a worry over the guard's attitude.
steps.whyThisMatters: If רבא is right, the משנה is not a dispute about הבטה at all, so רבה's proof that the question is argued by תנאים falls away. In this version, both sides of the משנה hold that הבטה does acquire.

phrases.english: Rava said: No,
everyone agrees
watching ownerless property acquires it,
and here, whether we are concerned
that perhaps he will not hand them over wholeheartedly
is what they argue about.
For the Rabbis hold:
we give him a wage,
and if not, we are concerned
that perhaps he will not hand them over wholeheartedly.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: לָא, דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא הַבָּטָה בְּהֶפְקֵר קָנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects רבה's reading (steps 22–26) of the משנה and offers another reason for the dispute.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the proof that the משנה is a dispute about whether הבטה acquires.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The dispute can be explained by a worry about the guard handing over the grain wholeheartedly, with everyone agreeing that הבטה acquires.

steps.title: רבי יוסי's side of רבא's explanation
steps.stepSummary: רבא finishes his explanation: רבי יוסי is not worried that an unpaid guard will hold back on handing over the grain.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי holds that we are not worried that perhaps the guard will not hand the grain over wholeheartedly.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes רבא's explanation by giving רבי יוסי's side. The ת״ק worried about an unpaid guard, and רבי יוסי does not share that worry.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In רבא's reading, both sides agree that the guard's looking acquires the grain for the community. The only question is trust. רבי יוסי trusts a volunteer guard to hand everything over fully, so in his view no payment is needed.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei holds
we are not concerned
that perhaps he will not hand them over wholeheartedly.
phrases.notes: 'Them' means the grain that the guard watched over for the community.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes רבא's rejection of רבה by stating רבי יוסי's side of the argument.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Completes רבא's replacement for רבה's explanation of the argument.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The argument is not about whether הבטה acquires. It is about whether we trust an unpaid guard.

steps.title: What did the Sages mean by 'you say so'?
steps.stepSummary: Under רבא's reading, the גמרא asks how to understand the חכמים's words to רבי יוסי, 'אתה אומר כן'.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what does 'you say so' mean?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks the same question it asked about רבה's reading, now under רבא's reading. It wants to know how the חכמים's words 'אתה אומר' fit this explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Any explanation of the argument must also make sense of the חכמים's reply to רבי יוסי in the משנה. So the גמרא checks whether רבא's reading can explain that reply too.

keyTerms.meaning: 'You say', the start of the חכמים's objection to רבי יוסי

phrases.english: And what is the meaning of 'you say'?
phrases.notes: This is the חכמים's 'if you say so...' to רבי יוסי in the משנה. The גמרא already asked this in step 25, following רבה's reading.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests רבא's reading against the wording of the משנה, the same way step 25 tested רבה's reading.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How the words 'אתה אומר כן' fit רבא's explanation.

steps.title: Combining both views means the offerings are not communal
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים told רבי יוסי: if we combine your ruling that a volunteer may guard with our worry that he will not hand the grain over fully, the עומר and שתי הלחם would not come from communal property.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what they were telling him: if we take your view, that a volunteer may guard, and add our view, that we worry he will not hand over the grain fully, then the עומר and the two loaves would not come from communal property.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the חכמים were combining two ideas. They added רבי יוסי's allowance for a volunteer guard to their own worry about an unpaid guard.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer has the same structure as step 26, but the worry being combined is different. If an unpaid guard might keep some grain back, the grain is not fully the community's. Then the עומר and שתי הלחם, which must be communal offerings, would be disqualified.

keyTerms.meaning: From your words to our words: combining your ruling with our view
The barley offering brought on the 16th of ניסן
The two wheat loaves offered on שבועות

steps.whatToRemember: In רבא's first version, everyone holds that הבטה acquires. Paying the guard makes sure he hands everything over to the community, so the offerings truly belong to the community.

phrases.english: This is what they were saying to him:
From your words to our words,
phrases.notes: He means: take your ruling and add it to our view.

phrases.english: that we are concerned
that perhaps he will not hand them over wholeheartedly:
the omer and the two loaves would not
come from communal property.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 29 by reading the חכמים's words as a combination of the two views.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The חכמים meant that a volunteer guard, together with the worry that he will not hand over the grain fully, means the offerings would not be communal.

steps.title: Second version: the payment scares off violent people
steps.stepSummary: In another version of רבא, everyone agrees that looking does not acquire ownerless property. The argument is whether the חכמים set up a payment for the guard so that violent people would hear about it and stay away from the grain.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say that רבא said: Everyone agrees that looking at ownerless property does not acquire it. Here they argue about whether we worry about violent people. The ת״ק holds that the Sages set up a rule to pay the guard four זוז, so that violent people would hear about it and keep away from the grain. רבי יוסי holds that the Sages did not set up such a rule.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a different version of what רבא said. In this version, the payment has nothing to do with acquiring the grain. It is a public sign meant to keep thieves away.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here רבא agrees with רבי יוסי's view in רבה's reading, that הבטה does not acquire, and makes it everyone's view. The four זוז payment shows that the grain is Temple property, so strong people will not dare to take it. רבי יוסי says the חכמים never made this rule, so a volunteer guard is fine.

keyTerms.meaning: There are those who say: introduces another version
Violent people who take things by force
The Sages set up a rule

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two versions of רבא. In the first, everyone agrees that הבטה acquires. In the second, everyone agrees that it does not acquire, and the payment is only there to scare off thieves.
steps.whatToRemember: There are three explanations of the argument. רבה: whether הבטה acquires. רבא, first version: whether we trust an unpaid guard. רבא, second version: whether the Sages set up a payment to keep violent people away.

phrases.english: There are those who say,
Rava said:
Everyone agrees
that looking at ownerless property does not acquire it,
and here they disagree about whether we worry about violent people.
For the first tanna holds
that the Sages instituted
to give him four zuz,
so that violent people will hear
and keep away from them.
phrases.notes: 'Them' is the grain. Once they hear the Temple pays the guards, they know it is Temple grain.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yosei holds: they did not institute it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא דְאָמְרִי רָבָא אָמַר דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא הַבָּטָה בְּהֶפְקֵר לָא קָנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second version of רבא that replaces his first explanation of the argument in the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Everyone agrees that looking does not acquire ownerless property. The ת״ק holds that the Sages set up a payment to keep violent people away, and רבי יוסי holds that they did not.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that paying the guard can be explained without any question of acquiring the grain, as a public sign that protects Temple property.
